description: How Charles I went from defeated king to executed traitor in twelve months 1648–1649.
content_html:
Charles I’s Gamble: The Second Civil War

After his defeat in 1646, Charles I was not a prisoner in the modern sense — he retained considerable freedom to negotiate. He used this time not to reach a genuine settlement but to play different factions off against each other. In December 1647 he signed a secret treaty (the Engagement) with Scottish commissioners, promising to establish Presbyterianism in England for three years in exchange for a Scottish invasion on his behalf.

In 1648 a series of Royalist uprisings broke out across England — in Kent, Essex and Wales — coordinated with a Scottish invasion. This Second Civil War was suppressed with speed and ruthlessness. Cromwell crushed the Scots at the Battle of Preston in August 1648. To many in the army, the Second Civil War was worse than the first: Charles had knowingly invited foreign invasion and domestic rebellion after already being defeated. Army officers began to use the word “traitor” for their former king.

Key Fact

In December 1647 Charles signed the Engagement with the Scots, promising three years of Presbyterianism in exchange for a Scottish invasion. When this plan failed at Preston (August 1648), army hardliners concluded Charles could never be trusted in any peace settlement.

Pride’s Purge: December 1648

Despite the army’s hostility, Parliament’s Presbyterian majority continued to negotiate with Charles through the Newport Treaty talks. The army saw this as treachery. On 6 December 1648, Colonel Thomas Pride stationed soldiers at the entrance to the House of Commons and physically prevented around 140 Presbyterian MPs from taking their seats — an act of military purge known as Pride’s Purge. Many were arrested; others withdrew voluntarily. What remained was the Rump Parliament — a small minority of MPs who were willing to proceed against the King.

Trying a king presented enormous legal difficulties. In English law, the King was the source of justice — courts acted in his name. There was no legal precedent for a court judging the monarch. The Rump Parliament declared itself supreme and established the High Court of Justice. However, when the Lords refused to participate, the Rump proceeded without them. Many lawyers and contemporaries regarded the court as constitutionally illegitimate. John Bradshaw, the court’s president, wore a bullet-proof hat at the trial, fearing assassination.

The Trial of Charles I: January 1649

The trial ran from 20 to 27 January 1649. Charles refused to acknowledge the court’s authority. He argued that no court had the power to try a king, and that by accepting its jurisdiction he would legitimise a precedent that could destroy the English constitution. His silence in the face of charges was therefore a principled constitutional stand, not simple stubbornness. This refusal meant no defence was mounted and the proceedings became one-sided.

Charles was found guilty of making war upon his people and sentenced to death. On 30 January 1649, he was beheaded on a scaffold outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall. Eyewitnesses reported a groan from the crowd when the axe fell. Charles died with great dignity, insisting he died as a martyr for the Church of England and for the people, “a subject and a sovereign are clean different things.” His execution shocked the courts of Europe.

Key Fact

Charles I refused to recognise the court’s authority, arguing that no court had jurisdiction to try a king, whose authority came from God. He was executed on 30 January 1649 outside the Banqueting House, Whitehall.

Commonwealth Proclaimed: 1649

In the weeks after the execution the Rump Parliament abolished the monarchy and the House of Lords and proclaimed England a Commonwealth. This was a revolutionary act — England had become a republic. However, the Commonwealth rested on a narrowly-based parliament that lacked popular legitimacy. It faced immediate threats: Royalist resistance in Ireland led by the Catholic Confederacy, and in Scotland where Charles II was proclaimed king.

Historians remain divided on the regicide. Some (e.g. Sean Kelsey) argue Charles stage-managed the trial as a propaganda victory for royalism, knowing his refusal to plead would undermine the court’s legitimacy. Others (e.g. Blair Worden) emphasise the army’s determination that there could be no settlement while Charles lived — his duplicity in the Engagement had made a treaty impossible. Both perspectives agree that the trial was legally anomalous: constituted by a purged parliament, with the Lords excluded, and with most of the appointed judges absent on the day of sentencing. The regicide divided the English political nation and shocked Protestant Europe.
exam_tip_html: Questions on the regicide often link to earlier events. Show how the Second Civil War (and the Engagement) changed army attitudes to Charles, making the execution possible. Explain Pride’s Purge as the moment that removed obstacles. Then analyse the trial itself — including Charles’s constitutional refusal to plead. A strong answer explains not just what happened but why each step made the next one possible, rather than treating the execution as an inevitability from the start of the war.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Charles signed the secret Engagement in December 1647, inviting Scottish invasion; the Second Civil War was crushed at Preston (August 1648), convincing army officers Charles could never be trusted.
  • Pride’s Purge (6 December 1648) removed Presbyterian MPs, leaving the Rump Parliament to proceed with the trial; Charles refused to recognise the court’s authority.
  • Charles I was executed on 30 January 1649; Parliament then abolished the monarchy and House of Lords and proclaimed England a Commonwealth.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Pride's Purge in December 1648.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: One accurate feature with supporting detail. Example: Colonel Thomas Pride stationed soldiers outside the House of Commons on 6 December 1648 and prevented approximately 140 Presbyterian MPs from entering, leaving a Rump of MPs willing to proceed against the King.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the trial of Charles I in January 1649.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Feature 1: Charles refused to acknowledge the court's authority, arguing no court had jurisdiction to try a king whose authority came from God. Feature 2: The court was constituted only by the Rump Parliament — the Lords refused to participate — and many of the appointed judges were absent at sentencing, making the proceedings legally anomalous.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Charles I's Engagement with the Scots made his execution more likely.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains how the Engagement (secret deal with Scots for Presbyterian settlement) led to the Second Civil War, how Preston made army hardliners determined there could be no settlement while Charles lived, and how this directly produced Pride's Purge and the decision to put him on trial. Secure: Two linked reasons. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple.

practice_questions.text: The execution of Charles I in 1649 was inevitable once the Civil War began. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Argues against inevitability by showing multiple contingencies (Propositions of Newcastle 1646, Newport Treaty talks, Presbyterian majority opposition to execution) while explaining factors that made execution more likely over time (Engagement, Second Civil War, Pride's Purge). Reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Both sides examined. Developing: One side mainly. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Charles I refused to plead at his trial in January 1649.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains constitutional argument (no court has jurisdiction over a king), religious conviction (divine right), strategic calculation (refusal undermined the court's legitimacy), precedent concern (accepting the court would destroy constitutional monarchy). Secure: Two reasons developed. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the army supported the execution of Charles I in 1649.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains the army's experience of the Second Civil War, sense of religious mission, Presbyterian Parliament's continued negotiations, conviction that Charles could not be trusted, Pride's Purge as expression of army will. Secure: Two reasons. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple.

glossary_terms.definition: Secret agreement signed between Charles I and Scottish commissioners in December 1647, promising to establish Presbyterianism in England in exchange for Scottish military support.
A series of Royalist risings and a Scottish invasion in 1648, launched after Charles I's secret Engagement with the Scots, crushed by Cromwell and Fairfax.
Parliamentary army officer who, acting under army orders on 6 December 1648, prevented approximately 140 Presbyterian MPs from entering the House of Commons.
The army's purge of Parliament on 6 December 1648, removing Presbyterian MPs and leaving a Rump that would proceed with the trial of Charles I.
President of the High Court of Justice that tried Charles I, a lawyer who presided over the trial in January 1649.
The republic established in England in 1649 after the execution of Charles I, governed by the Rump Parliament and a Council of State.
